title: Frederik Godt
text:
I am a tenure-track assistant professor at the Department of Political Science, University of Southern Denmark, affiliated with the Public Administration Research Group. My research systematically examines how citizens’ encounters with the state shape their trust in public institutions. My primary contribution is to the understanding of the micro-foundations of institutional trust. Specifically, my research demonstrates that institutional trust is shaped by perceptions of outcomes, fair processes, and relations with frontline workers, and politicians’ ability to efficiently deliver on promised policy objectives. This research agenda has resulted in a series of publications in leading international journals and established my expertise in institutional trust and causal inference through survey experiments.
I received my PhD in political science at Aarhus University in November 2021.

Hansen, F. G. (2022). How Impressions of Public Employees’ Warmth and Competence Influence Trust in Government. International Public Management Journal, 25(6), 939–961. Journal version Open access



A central argument in the performance-trust literature is that the performance of public service delivery shapes citizen trust in government. However, studies have failed to address to what extent single interactions with public employees affect citizen trust in government. Building on insights from social psychology, this article argues that citizens spontaneously make impressions of the warmth (e.g., friendliness) and competence (e.g., effectiveness) of the public employee with whom they interact. Utilizing two large-scale randomized survey experiments, conducted in Denmark and the United States, this study demonstrates that impressions of warmth and competence in a concrete interaction with a public employee have important effects on general trust in civil servants. The findings further provide evidence that a single case experience can have implications for trust in broader administrative and political institutions of government. Thus, this article shows that even a single bureaucratic encounter can potentially have wide-ranging implications.
